claim: Deletion of the gene encoding PHLPP1 protects mice from lethal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge.
source: Here we report that deletion of the gene encoding PH domain Leucine-rich repeat Protein Phosphatase 1 (PHLPP1) protects mice from lethal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge and live Escherichia coli infection.
evidence: Supported by survival data from mouse experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Deletion of the gene encoding PHLPP1 protects mice from live Escherichia coli infection.
source: Here we report that deletion of the gene encoding PH domain Leucine-rich repeat Protein Phosphatase 1 (PHLPP1) protects mice from lethal lipopolysaccharide (LPS) challenge and live Escherichia coli infection.
evidence: Supported by survival data from mouse experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PHLPP1 controls the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling by dephosphorylating STAT1 on Ser727.
source: Investigation of PHLPP1 function in macrophages reveals that it controls the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling by dephosphorylating the transcription factor STAT1 on Ser727 to inhibit its activity, reduce its promoter residency, and reduce the expression of target genes involved in innate immunity and cytokine signaling.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A-B showing increased Ser727 phosphorylation in Phlpp1-/- cells, in vitro phosphatase assay in Figure 4C, and ChIP data in Figure 3D-F showing increased STAT1 promoter binding.

claim: PHLPP1 dephosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 inhibits STAT1 transcriptional activity.
source: Investigation of PHLPP1 function in macrophages reveals that it controls the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling by dephosphorylating the transcription factor STAT1 on Ser727 to inhibit its activity, reduce its promoter residency, and reduce the expression of target genes involved in innate immunity and cytokine signaling.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assays in Figure 6A and 6C showing increased STAT1 promoter activity in Phlpp1-/- cells and decreased activity upon PHLPP1 overexpression.

claim: PHLPP1 dephosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 reduces STAT1 promoter residency.
source: Investigation of PHLPP1 function in macrophages reveals that it controls the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling by dephosphorylating the transcription factor STAT1 on Ser727 to inhibit its activity, reduce its promoter residency, and reduce the expression of target genes involved in innate immunity and cytokine signaling.
evidence: Supported by ChIP data in Figure 3D-F showing enhanced and sustained STAT1 binding to promoters in Phlpp1-/- macrophages.

claim: PHLPP1 dephosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 reduces the expression of target genes involved in innate immunity and cytokine signaling.
source: Investigation of PHLPP1 function in macrophages reveals that it controls the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling by dephosphorylating the transcription factor STAT1 on Ser727 to inhibit its activity, reduce its promoter residency, and reduce the expression of target genes involved in innate immunity and cytokine signaling.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 2A showing 199 genes with elevated expression in Phlpp1-/- macrophages, and qPCR data in Figure 2E-G and Figure 3A-C showing increased expression of specific target genes.

claim: PHLPP1 function in controlling inflammatory signaling depends on a bipartite nuclear localization signal in its unique N-terminal extension.
source: This previously undescribed function of PHLPP1 depends on a bipartite nuclear localization signal in its unique N-terminal extension.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6E-F showing nuclear localization of NTE constructs, and luciferase assays in Figure 6G showing that NLS mutations abolish PHLPP1's ability to suppress STAT1 activity.

claim: Nuclear PHLPP1 dephosphorylates STAT1 to control the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling in macrophages.
source: Our data support a model in which nuclear PHLPP1 dephosphorylates STAT1 to control the magnitude and duration of inflammatory signaling in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by multiple lines of evidence including phosphorylation data (Figure 4), promoter binding data (Figure 3D-F), transcriptional activity assays (Figure 6), and nuclear localization studies (Figure 6E-F).

claim: At a dose where more than 50% of WT mice died within 12 hr of E. coli challenge, 50% of the Phlpp1-/- mice remained alive after 10 days.
source: Surprisingly, absence of PHLPP1 provided a strong protective effect; at a dose where more than 50% of WT mice died within 12 hr of E. coli challenge, 50% of the Phlpp1-/- mice remained alive after 10 days (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nearly half of the Phlpp1-/- mice were alive after 10 days following LPS injection compared to only 1 out of 16 of the WT mice.
source: Similarly, Phlpp1-/- mice were protected from toxicity induced by the purified Gram-negative bacterial cell wall component LPS, with nearly half of the Phlpp1-/- mice alive after 10 days compared to only 1 out of 16 of the WT mice (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly supported by survival curve data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Serum levels of IL-6 were significantly increased in WT mice within 5 hr of LPS injection, returning to baseline within 12 hr.
source: Serum levels of pro-inflammatory cytokine interleukin 6 (IL-6) were significantly increased in WT mice within 5 hr of LPS injection, returning to baseline within 12 hr (Figure 1C).
evidence: Directly supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Phlpp1-/- mice had 2-fold lower IL-6 levels at 5 hr post-infection compared to WT mice.
source: In contrast, the Phlpp1-/- mice had 2-fold lower IL-6 levels at 5 hr post-infection, but these levels were sustained for up to 24 hr, suggestive of improper resolution of inflammation.
evidence: Directly supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: IL-6 levels in Phlpp1-/- mice were sustained for up to 24 hr post-infection, suggestive of improper resolution of inflammation.
source: In contrast, the Phlpp1-/- mice had 2-fold lower IL-6 levels at 5 hr post-infection, but these levels were sustained for up to 24 hr, suggestive of improper resolution of inflammation.
evidence: Directly supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1C and interpreted by the authors.

claim: Levels of IL-1β were consistently higher in Phlpp1-/- mice compared with WT mice.
source: Levels of another pro-inflammatory cytokine, IL-1β, were likewise consistently higher in Phlpp1-/- mice compared with WT mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Directly supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Levels of IL-10 did not differ significantly between WT and Phlpp1-/- mice.
source: By contrast, levels of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 did not differ significantly between the WT and Phlpp1-/- mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Directly supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: PHLPP1 plays an essential role in regulation of the innate immune response at the whole organism level.
source: These findings indicate an essential role for PHLPP1 in regulation of the innate immune response at the whole organism level.
evidence: Inferred from the survival and cytokine data presented in Figure 1.

claim: RNA-Seq analysis identified 1,654 mRNA transcripts induced more than two-fold by KLA treatment with FDR less than 0.05.
source: RNA-Seq analysis identified 1,654 mRNA transcripts induced more than two-fold by KLA treatment, with a false discovery rate (FDR) less than 0.05 at any of the time points.
evidence: Directly supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expression of approximately 12% of KLA-induced genes (199 genes) was increased in macrophages from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to WT mice 6 hr following KLA treatment.
source: Expression of approximately 12% of these genes (199 genes; Supplementary file 1) was increased in macrophages from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to those from littermate control WT mice 6 hr following KLA treatment; transcript levels of these genes remained significantly elevated (>two fold) 24 hr later.
evidence: Directly supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A and listed in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Transcript levels of 199 genes elevated in Phlpp1-/- macrophages remained significantly elevated (>two fold) 24 hr after KLA treatment.
source: Expression of approximately 12% of these genes (199 genes; Supplementary file 1) was increased in macrophages from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to those from littermate control WT mice 6 hr following KLA treatment; transcript levels of these genes remained significantly elevated (>two fold) 24 hr later.
evidence: Directly supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A and listed in Supplementary file 1.

claim: 144 genes exhibited reduced expression 24 hr following KLA treatment in Phlpp1-/- macrophages compared to WT.
source: Another set of genes exhibited reduced expression 24 hr following KLA treatment (144 genes; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Directly supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 2A and listed in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Many genes with elevated expression in Phlpp1-/- macrophages are associated with inflammatory signaling pathways including innate immune response, cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, LPS signaling, interferon-β response, and TNF signaling.
source: Gene ontology analysis revealed that many of the genes whose expression was elevated in the Phlpp1-/- macrophages are associated with inflammatory signaling: these included genes annotated for their involvement in the innate immune response, cytokine-cytokine receptor interactions, LPS signaling, interferon-β response, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling-dependent pathways (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Genes significantly decreased in Phlpp1-/- compared to WT macrophages were enriched most significantly in nodes related to central carbon metabolism.
source: Genes significantly decreased in Phlpp1-/- compared to WT macrophages were enriched most significantly in nodes related to central carbon metabolism, and to a lesser extent, chronic inflammatory responses and LPS signaling (Figure 2B).
evidence: Directly supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: De novo motif analysis revealed significant enrichment of STAT (p<10−18) and IRF (p<10−9) motifs in promoters of genes with elevated expression in Phlpp1-/- macrophages.
source: The analysis revealed significant enrichment of STAT (p<10−18) and IRF (p<10−9) motifs (Figure 2C) in the promoters of genes whose expression was statistically increased in Phlpp1-/- macrophages compared to WT macrophages.
evidence: Directly supported by HOMER motif analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Of the 199 genes with elevated expression in Phlpp1-/- macrophages, 46% had promoters with a consensus STAT binding motif.
source: Of the 199 genes with elevated expression, 46% of the genes had promoters with a consensus STAT binding motif, 51% had promoters with a potential binding site for IRF family of transcription factors, and 26% had promoters with predicted binding sites for both STAT and IRF (Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: 51% of the 199 genes with elevated expression in Phlpp1-/- macrophages had promoters with a potential binding site for IRF family of transcription factors.
source: Of the 199 genes with elevated expression, 46% of the genes had promoters with a consensus STAT binding motif, 51% had promoters with a potential binding site for IRF family of transcription factors, and 26% had promoters with predicted binding sites for both STAT and IRF (Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: 26% of the 199 genes with elevated expression in Phlpp1-/- macrophages had promoters with predicted binding sites for both STAT and IRF.
source: Of the 199 genes with elevated expression, 46% of the genes had promoters with a consensus STAT binding motif, 51% had promoters with a potential binding site for IRF family of transcription factors, and 26% had promoters with predicted binding sites for both STAT and IRF (Figure 2D).
evidence: Directly supported by motif analysis data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: STAT1 is required for LPS-induced gene expression in macrophages.
source: STAT1 is required for LPS-induced gene expression in macrophages (Ohmori and Hamilton, 2001) and implicated as a PHLPP1 target in iNOS regulation (Alamuru et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Ohmori and Hamilton, 2001; Alamuru et al., 2014).

claim: STAT1 knockdown by siRNA resulted in a 2-fold reduction in KLA-induced transcription of Cd69, Ifit2, and Gbp5 at 6 hr compared to control siRNA transfection.
source: STAT1 knockdown by siRNA in thioglycollate-elicited peritoneal macrophages resulted in a 2-fold reduction in KLA-induced transcription of Cd69, Ifit2, and Gbp5 at 6 hr compared to a control siRNA transfection, with transcript levels dropping to near baseline by 24 hr (Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Directly supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: KLA induced STAT1 binding to the promoters of Cd69, Ifit2, and Gbp5, with maximal binding observed 1 hr post stimulation.
source: KLA induced STAT1 binding to the promoters of Cd69, Ifit2, and Gbp5, with maximal binding observed 1 hr post stimulation, followed by a decay in binding to near baseline after 24 hr (Figure 3D–F).
evidence: Directly supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: STAT1 binding to the promoters of Cd69, Ifit2, and Gbp5 was enhanced and sustained in Phlpp1-/- macrophages relative to WT cells.
source: In contrast, binding to these promoters was enhanced and sustained in Phlpp1-/- macrophages relative to WT cells.
evidence: Directly supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: PHLPP1 suppresses KLA-stimulated binding of STAT1 to its promoters and thereby reduces transcription of its target genes.
source: Thus, PHLPP1 suppresses KLA-stimulated binding of STAT1 to its promoters and thereby reduces transcription of its target genes.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing increased STAT1 promoter binding (Figure 3D-F) and increased gene expression (Figure 2E-G, Figure 3A-C) in Phlpp1-/- cells.

claim: Loss of PHLPP1 in BMDMs led to a robust increase in STAT1 phosphorylation on Ser727.
source: Loss of PHLPP1 in BMDMs led to a robust increase in STAT1 phosphorylation on the regulatory site Ser727 but did not affect Tyr701 phosphorylation (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Loss of PHLPP1 in BMDMs did not affect STAT1 phosphorylation on Tyr701.
source: Loss of PHLPP1 in BMDMs led to a robust increase in STAT1 phosphorylation on the regulatory site Ser727 but did not affect Tyr701 phosphorylation (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: PHLPP1 loss resulted in an increase in Erk phosphorylation at its activation loop sites.
source: PHLPP1 loss also resulted in an increase in Erk phosphorylation at its activation loop sites, as previously reported (Reyes et al., 2014).
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4A-B and cited prior work (Reyes et al., 2014).

claim: Incubation of in vitro phosphorylated STAT1 with immunoprecipitated FLAG-tagged PHLPP1 resulted in dephosphorylation at Ser727.
source: Incubation of in vitro phosphorylated STAT1 with immunoprecipitated FLAG-tagged PHLPP1 resulted in dephosphorylation at Ser727, suggesting that PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates STAT1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Directly supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates STAT1 at Ser727.
source: Incubation of in vitro phosphorylated STAT1 with immunoprecipitated FLAG-tagged PHLPP1 resulted in dephosphorylation at Ser727, suggesting that PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates STAT1 (Figure 4C).
evidence: Directly supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Overexpression of PHLPP1 in HEK-293T cells reduced IFNγ-dependent phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of PHLPP1 in HEK-293T cells reduced IFNγ-dependent phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 but not on Tyr701 (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Overexpression of PHLPP1 in HEK-293T cells did not affect IFNγ-dependent phosphorylation of STAT1 on Tyr701.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of PHLPP1 in HEK-293T cells reduced IFNγ-dependent phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 but not on Tyr701 (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: PHLPP1 selectively dephosphorylates the Ser727 regulatory phosphorylation on STAT1 in vitro and in cells.
source: Thus, PHLPP1 selectively dephosphorylates the Ser727 regulatory phosphorylation on STAT1 in vitro and in cells.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing PHLPP1 dephosphorylates Ser727 but not Tyr701 in multiple experimental systems (Figure 4).

claim: The KLA-induced increase in Ser727 phosphorylation was relatively insensitive to okadaic acid.
source: Figure 5A–B shows that the KLA-induced increase in Ser727 phosphorylation was relatively insensitive to OA, under conditions where the phosphorylation of Erk (at Thr202/Tyr204) and Akt (at Thr308) was significantly increased upon OA addition.
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Phosphorylation of Erk at Thr202/Tyr204 was significantly increased upon okadaic acid addition.
source: Figure 5A–B shows that the KLA-induced increase in Ser727 phosphorylation was relatively insensitive to OA, under conditions where the phosphorylation of Erk (at Thr202/Tyr204) and Akt (at Thr308) was significantly increased upon OA addition.
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: Phosphorylation of Akt at Thr308 was significantly increased upon okadaic acid addition.
source: Figure 5A–B shows that the KLA-induced increase in Ser727 phosphorylation was relatively insensitive to OA, under conditions where the phosphorylation of Erk (at Thr202/Tyr204) and Akt (at Thr308) was significantly increased upon OA addition.
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A-B.

claim: PHLPP1 is the primary regulator of phosphorylation on the Ser727 site of STAT1.
source: These data are consistent with PHLPP1, a PP2C family member, being the primary regulator of phosphorylation on the activity-tuning Ser727 site of STAT1.
evidence: Inferred from the okadaic acid insensitivity data (Figure 5) combined with other evidence showing PHLPP1 specifically regulates Ser727 phosphorylation.

claim: STAT1 promoter activity was significantly higher in Phlpp1-/- MEFs compared to WT MEFs at both 6 hr and 24 hr following IFNγ stimulation.
source: Figure 6A shows that STAT1 promoter activity was significantly higher in Phlpp1-/- MEFs compared to WT MEFs at both 6 hr and 24 hr.
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Pre-treatment of cells with okadaic acid had no effect on STAT1 promoter activity.
source: Pre-treatment of cells with okadaic acid, under conditions that increased the phosphorylation of PP2A-sensitive substrates (see Figure 5A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1), had no effect on STAT1 promoter activity (Figure 6A)
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The overexpressed PP2C domain of PHLPP1 was considerably less effective in inhibiting STAT1 promoter activity compared to full-length PHLPP1.
source: The overexpressed PP2C domain of PHLPP1 (Figure 6C, blue) was considerably less effective in inhibiting STAT1 promoter activity compared to full-length PHLPP1 (Figure 6C, red).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Forcing the PP2C domain into the nucleus by attaching an NLS to its N-terminus inhibited STAT1 promoter activity as effectively as overexpression of full-length PHLPP1.
source: However, forcing the PP2C domain into the nucleus by attaching an NLS to its N-terminus inhibited STAT1 promoter activity as effectively as overexpression of full-length PHLPP1 (Figure 6C, orange).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The catalytically-inactive NLS-PP2C was no longer able to suppress STAT1 activity.
source: The catalytically-inactive NLS-PP2C was no longer able to suppress STAT1 activity (Figure 6C, purple)
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C using the DDAA mutant.

claim: Both the catalytic activity and nuclear localization of PHLPP1 are necessary for it to regulate STAT1 transcriptional activity.
source: Thus, both the catalytic activity and nuclear localization of PHLPP1 are necessary for it to regulate STAT1 transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined luciferase assay data in Figure 6C showing that both nuclear targeting and catalytic activity are required.

claim: Bioinformatics analysis of the sequence of PHLPP1 using SeqNLS revealed a potential Arg-rich bipartite NLS (92RRRRR-X-122RRGRLKR) in the N-terminal extension unique to the PHLPP1 isozyme.
source: Bioinformatics analysis of the sequence of PHLPP1 using SeqNLS (Lin and Hu, 2013) revealed a potential Arg-rich bipartite NLS (92RRRRR-X-122RRGRLKR) in the N-terminal extension unique to the PHLPP1 isozyme (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis using SeqNLS software (Lin and Hu, 2013).

claim: The NTE of PHLPP1 localizes to the nucleus.
source: Immunofluorescence revealed that the NTE localizes to the nucleus.
evidence: Directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Mutation of the first NLS or the second NLS increased the distribution of the NTE to the cytosol.
source: Mutation of the first NLS or the second NLS increased the distribution of the NTE to the cytosol, and mutation of both decreased the nuclear:cytoplasmic ratio to be comparable to that of a construct of the NTE with a strong Nuclear Export Signal (NES) (LALKLAGLDI from PKI; see Wen et al., 1995a) (Figure 6F).
evidence: Directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6E-F.

claim: Full-length PHLPP1 was primarily cytosolic.
source: Full-length PHLPP1 was primarily cytosolic, leading us to ask whether there may also be an NES.
evidence: Directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Bioinformatics analysis of the primary sequence identified a potential Leu-rich NES immediately following the last LRR and preceding the phosphatase domain.
source: Bioinformatics analysis of the primary sequence identified a potential Leu-rich NES (Xu et al., 2015) immediately following the last LRR and preceding the phosphatase domain (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis using methods from Xu et al., 2015.

claim: Attachment of the 14-residue NES sequence to the N-terminus of the NTE resulted in distribution of the NTE to the cytosol.
source: Attachment of this 14-residue sequence to the N-terminus of the NTE resulted in distribution of the NTE to the cytosol (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: PHLPP1 nuclear localization is controlled by a bipartite NLS in the NTE and is opposed by an NES following the LRR.
source: Thus, PHLPP1 nuclear localization is controlled by a bipartite NLS in the NTE and is opposed by an NES following the LRR.
evidence: Inferred from the combined immunofluorescence data showing NLS function (Figure 6E-F) and NES function (Figure 6—figure supplement 4).

claim: The reduction in IFNγ-induced STAT1 activity resulting from PHLPP1 overexpression was abolished upon mutation of NLS2.
source: The reduction in IFNγ-induced STAT1 activity resulting from PHLPP1 overexpression (Figure 6G, red) was abolished upon mutation of NLS2 (Figure 6G, brown) or both halves of the NLS (NLS1/2) (Figure 6G, purple).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The reduction in IFNγ-induced STAT1 activity resulting from PHLPP1 overexpression was abolished upon mutation of both halves of the NLS (NLS1/2).
source: The reduction in IFNγ-induced STAT1 activity resulting from PHLPP1 overexpression (Figure 6G, red) was abolished upon mutation of NLS2 (Figure 6G, brown) or both halves of the NLS (NLS1/2) (Figure 6G, purple).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Mutation of NLS1 had an intermediate effect on PHLPP1's ability to reduce STAT1 activity.
source: Mutation of NLS1 had an intermediate effect (Figure 6G, blue).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: A bipartite NLS in the NTE of PHLPP1 localizes PHLPP1 to the nucleus, where it suppresses the transcriptional activity of STAT1.
source: These data reveal that a bipartite NLS in the NTE of PHLPP1 localizes PHLPP1 to the nucleus, where it suppresses the transcriptional activity of STAT1.
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing NLS function (Figure 6E-F) and requirement for STAT1 regulation (Figure 6G).

claim: Overexpression of full-length PHLPP1 in HEK-293T cells markedly reduced GAS promoter activity compared to vector only control.
source: Overexpression of full-length PHLPP1 in HEK-293T cells markedly reduced GAS promoter activity (Figure 7A, red) compared to the vector only control (Figure 7A, black).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A construct of PHLPP1 lacking the NTE was less effective than full-length PHLPP1 in reducing STAT1 activity.
source: A construct of PHLPP1 lacking the NTE (deletion of first 512 amino acids of its N-terminus; PHLPP1ΔNTE, blue) was less effective than full-length PHLPP1 in reducing STAT1 activity
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: A construct comprised of just the NTE caused a significant increase in GAS promoter activity, suggesting a dominant-negative function of this segment.
source: whereas a construct comprised of just the NTE (amino acids 1–512, green) caused a significant increase in GAS promoter activity, suggesting a dominant-negative function of this segment.
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7A and interpreted by the authors.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation assays revealed a robust interaction of STAT1 with the immunoprecipitated NTE of PHLPP1.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assays revealed a robust interaction of STAT1 with the immunoprecipitated NTE of PHLPP1, in contrast to barely detectable binding of STAT1 to PHLPP1 lacking the NTE (Figure 7B).
evidence: Directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Barely detectable binding of STAT1 to PHLPP1 lacking the NTE was observed.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation assays revealed a robust interaction of STAT1 with the immunoprecipitated NTE of PHLPP1, in contrast to barely detectable binding of STAT1 to PHLPP1 lacking the NTE (Figure 7B).
evidence: Directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Intermediate binding was observed between STAT1 and full-length PHLPP1.
source: Intermediate binding was observed between STAT1 and full-length PHLPP1.
evidence: Directly supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The isolated NTE of PHLPP1 binds STAT1 approximately five times more strongly than full-length PHLPP1.
source: Quantification of three independent experiments revealed that the isolated NTE of PHLPP1 binds STAT1 approximately five times more strongly than full-length PHLPP1 and 26 times more strongly than PHLPP1 lacking the NTE (Figure 7C).
evidence: Directly supported by quantification of co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The isolated NTE of PHLPP1 binds STAT1 26 times more strongly than PHLPP1 lacking the NTE.
source: Quantification of three independent experiments revealed that the isolated NTE of PHLPP1 binds STAT1 approximately five times more strongly than full-length PHLPP1 and 26 times more strongly than PHLPP1 lacking the NTE (Figure 7C).
evidence: Directly supported by quantification of co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The NTE of PHLPP1 interacts with STAT1 and reduces its promoter activity.
source: These data reveal that the NTE of PHLPP1 interacts with STAT1 and reduces its promoter activity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined co-immunoprecipitation data (Figure 7B-C) and luciferase assay data (Figure 7A).

claim: Phlpp1-/- mice are protected from LPS-induced death.
source: The finding that Phlpp1-/- mice are protected from LPS-induced death allowed us to identify PHLPP1 as a physiologically relevant phosphatase in the overall innate immune response.
evidence: Supported by survival data in Figure 1B.

claim: PHLPP1 is a physiologically relevant phosphatase in the overall innate immune response.
source: The finding that Phlpp1-/- mice are protected from LPS-induced death allowed us to identify PHLPP1 as a physiologically relevant phosphatase in the overall innate immune response.
evidence: Inferred from the survival data in Figure 1 and the mechanistic studies in macrophages.

claim: The immunoregulatory phenotype of Phlpp1-/- mice likely reflects roles of PHLPP1 in several immune cell types.
source: It is likely that this immunoregulatory phenotype reflects roles of PHLPP1 in several immune cell types, and future studies of mice with cell-specific deletions of Phlpp1 will be of great interest.
evidence: Speculative statement by the authors based on the whole organism phenotype.

claim: Investigation of Phlpp1-/- macrophages indicates a significant role in counter-regulation of STAT1-dependent transcription that emerges as a secondary response to TLR4 ligation.
source: Investigation of Phlpp1-/- macrophages indicates a significant role in counter-regulation of STAT1-dependent transcription that emerges as a secondary response to TLR4 ligation.
evidence: Supported by the RNA-Seq data (Figure 2), ChIP data (Figure 3), and mechanistic studies (Figures 4-7).

claim: PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates Ser727 on STAT1 in vitro.
source: Specifically, PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates Ser727 on STAT1 in vitro and specifically suppresses phosphorylation of Ser727, but not Tyr701, on STAT1 in cells, correlating to decreased transcriptional activity of STAT1 at one of its major binding sites, the GAS promoter.
evidence: Directly supported by in vitro phosphatase assay data in Figure 4C.

claim: PHLPP1 specifically suppresses phosphorylation of Ser727, but not Tyr701, on STAT1 in cells.
source: Specifically, PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates Ser727 on STAT1 in vitro and specifically suppresses phosphorylation of Ser727, but not Tyr701, on STAT1 in cells, correlating to decreased transcriptional activity of STAT1 at one of its major binding sites, the GAS promoter.
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data in Figure 4A-B and 4D-E.

claim: PHLPP1 suppression of Ser727 phosphorylation correlates to decreased transcriptional activity of STAT1 at the GAS promoter.
source: Specifically, PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylates Ser727 on STAT1 in vitro and specifically suppresses phosphorylation of Ser727, but not Tyr701, on STAT1 in cells, correlating to decreased transcriptional activity of STAT1 at one of its major binding sites, the GAS promoter.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data in Figure 6A and 6C.

claim: The intrinsic catalytic activity of PHLPP1 is required for transcriptional regulation of STAT1.
source: The intrinsic catalytic activity and nuclear localization of PHLPP1 is required for this transcriptional regulation
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 6C showing the DDAA mutant cannot suppress STAT1 activity.

claim: Nuclear localization of PHLPP1 is required for transcriptional regulation of STAT1.
source: The intrinsic catalytic activity and nuclear localization of PHLPP1 is required for this transcriptional regulation
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 6C showing that nuclear targeting is necessary for STAT1 regulation.

claim: While the isolated PP2C domain is not efficient in suppressing GAS promoter activity, forcing the PP2C domain into the nucleus is as effective as the full-length phosphatase in controlling transcriptional activity.
source: while the isolated PP2C domain is not efficient in suppressing GAS promoter activity, forcing the PP2C domain into the nucleus is as effective as the full-length phosphatase in controlling transcriptional activity.
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 6C.

claim: Nuclear localization of the full-length enzyme is driven by a bipartite NLS identified in the NTE.
source: Nuclear localization of the full-length enzyme is driven by a bipartite NLS we identify in the NTE.
evidence: Supported by bioinformatics analysis (Figure 6D), immunofluorescence data (Figure 6E-F), and functional data (Figure 6G).

claim: Elimination of PHLPP1 results in global changes in KLA-dependent transcriptional regulation.
source: Elimination of PHLPP1 results in global changes in KLA-dependent transcriptional regulation, with 20% of the approximately 2000 genes whose expression changes upon KLA stimulation differing by more than two-fold in BMDMs from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to WT mice.
evidence: Directly supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 2A.

claim: 20% of the approximately 2000 genes whose expression changes upon KLA stimulation differ by more than two-fold in BMDMs from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to WT mice.
source: Elimination of PHLPP1 results in global changes in KLA-dependent transcriptional regulation, with 20% of the approximately 2000 genes whose expression changes upon KLA stimulation differing by more than two-fold in BMDMs from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to WT mice.
evidence: Directly supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 2A showing 199 elevated and 144 decreased genes out of 1654 total KLA-regulated genes.

claim: Phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 has been proposed to occur following the binding of the Tyr-phosphorylated STAT1 dimer to chromatin.
source: Phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727 has been proposed to occur following the binding of the Tyr-phosphorylated STAT1 dimer to chromatin (Sadzak et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Sadzak et al., 2008).

claim: Ser727 phosphorylation on the C-terminal transactivation domain of STAT1 is necessary for maximal transcriptional activity.
source: Ser727 phosphorylation on the C-terminal transactivation domain of STAT1 is necessary for maximal transcriptional activity.
evidence: Represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Identification of PHLPP1 as a phosphatase that opposes Ser727 phosphorylation provides a mechanism to counter-regulate the activity of STAT1.
source: Identification of PHLPP1 as a phosphatase that opposes this phosphorylation provides a mechanism to counter-regulate the activity of this key transcription factor.
evidence: Inferred from the combined mechanistic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Genetic depletion of PHLPP1 increases both STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation and transcriptional activity at the GAS promoter.
source: First, genetic depletion of PHLPP1 increases both STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation and transcriptional activity at the GAS promoter
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4A-B and luciferase assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: PHLPP1 overexpression decreases both STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation and transcriptional activity at the promoter.
source: whereas PHLPP1 overexpression decreases both STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation and transcriptional activity at the promoter.
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4D-E and luciferase assay data in Figure 6C.

claim: Both the IFNγ-induced phosphorylation of Ser727 and resulting increase in transcriptional activity at the GAS promoter are insensitive to okadaic acid.
source: Second, both the IFNγ-induced phosphorylation of Ser727 and resulting increase in transcriptional activity at the GAS promoter are insensitive to OA, a phosphatase inhibitor that is ineffective towards PP2C family members but highly effective towards the abundant PP2A in cells.
evidence: Directly supported by western blot data in Figure 5A-B and luciferase assay data in Figure 6A.

claim: Okadaic acid is a phosphatase inhibitor that is ineffective towards PP2C family members but highly effective towards the abundant PP2A in cells.
source: Second, both the IFNγ-induced phosphorylation of Ser727 and resulting increase in transcriptional activity at the GAS promoter are insensitive to OA, a phosphatase inhibitor that is ineffective towards PP2C family members but highly effective towards the abundant PP2A in cells.
evidence: Represents established knowledge about okadaic acid specificity.

claim: The insensitivity of STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation to okadaic acid is consistent with PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylating this site in cells.
source: The insensitivity of STAT1 Ser727 phosphorylation to OA is consistent with PHLPP1 directly dephosphorylating this site in cells, a reaction it catalyzes in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the okadaic acid insensitivity data (Figure 5) and in vitro phosphatase assay (Figure 4C).

claim: PHLPP1's effect on STAT1 is unlikely to involve Akt because Akt activity is sensitive to okadaic acid.
source: Furthermore, although PHLPP1 does suppress the signaling output of Akt (by dephosphorylating Ser473; see Gao et al., 2005) and Erk (by reducing the steady-state levels of RTKs; see Reyes et al., 2014), its effect on STAT1 is unlikely to involve either of these targets because the activities of both kinases are sensitive to OA.
evidence: Inferred from the okadaic acid sensitivity data in Figure 5 combined with prior knowledge about PHLPP1 substrates.

claim: PHLPP1's effect on STAT1 is unlikely to involve Erk because Erk activity is sensitive to okadaic acid.
source: Furthermore, although PHLPP1 does suppress the signaling output of Akt (by dephosphorylating Ser473; see Gao et al., 2005) and Erk (by reducing the steady-state levels of RTKs; see Reyes et al., 2014), its effect on STAT1 is unlikely to involve either of these targets because the activities of both kinases are sensitive to OA.
evidence: Inferred from the okadaic acid sensitivity data in Figure 5 combined with prior knowledge about PHLPP1 substrates.

claim: The effects of PHLPP1 on Ser727 are not a result of PHLPP1 reducing PKC steady-state levels.
source: Nor are the effects on Ser727 a result of PHLPP1 reducing PKC steady-state levels (Baffi et al., 2019; Gao et al., 2008), as the general PKC inhibitor Gö6983 did not alter GAS promoter activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Directly supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genetic depletion of PHLPP1 or STAT1 has opposing effects on transcriptional targets of STAT1.
source: Third, genetic depletion of either PHLPP1 or STAT1 has opposing effects on transcriptional targets of STAT1: whereas KLA causes a larger increase in mRNA of Cd69, Ifit2, and Gbp5 in BMDMs from Phlpp1-/- mice compared to WT mice, a reduction in these transcripts is observed upon STAT1 knockdown.
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 2E-G and qPCR data in Figure 3A-C.

claim: PHLPP1 regulates transcription of genes and binds chromatin.
source: Lastly, we have previously shown that PHLPP1 regulates transcription of genes and binds chromatin (Reyes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Reyes et al., 2014).

claim: PHLPP1 is the major phosphatase to oppose the activating phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727.
source: Cumulatively, these data are consistent with PHLPP1 being the major phosphatase to oppose the activating phosphorylation of STAT1 on Ser727, thereby limiting its transcriptional activity.
evidence: Inferred from the cumulative evidence presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The interaction of PHLPP1 with STAT1, mediated by its NTE, affords fidelity and specificity in its dephosphorylation of the transcription factor.
source: The interaction of PHLPP1 with STAT1, mediated by its NTE, affords fidelity and specificity in its dephosphorylation of the transcription factor.
evidence: Inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7B-C showing NTE-mediated binding.

claim: PHLPP1 binding to STAT1 is consistent with this multi-valent protein utilizing its protein-interaction domains to position it near its substrates.
source: PHLPP1 binding to STAT1 is consistent with this multi-valent protein utilizing its protein-interaction domains to position it near its substrates, either via direct interaction or by binding protein scaffolds, such as PDZ domain proteins that coordinate Akt signaling (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: Inferred from the current data and prior knowledge about PHLPP1 function cited from Li et al., 2011.

claim: PHLPP1 has a low catalytic activity of approximately one reaction per sec towards peptide substrates, over an order of magnitude lower than that of the related phosphatase PP2Cα.
source: Such coordination is essential for its dephosphorylation of relevant substrates, in part due to the low catalytic activity of the phosphatase (approximately one reaction per sec towards peptide substrates, over an order of magnitude lower than that of the related phosphatase PP2Cα; see Sierecki and Newton, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Sierecki and Newton, 2014).

claim: Deletion of the last three amino acids of PHLPP1 to remove the PDZ ligand abolishes the ability of PHLPP1 to dephosphorylate Akt in cells.
source: The importance of enzyme proximity to its substrate is best illustrated with Akt, where deletion of the last three amino acids of PHLPP1 to remove the PDZ ligand abolishes the ability of PHLPP1 to dephosphorylate Akt in cells (Gao et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Gao et al., 2005).

claim: Binding of PHLPP1 via its NTE to STAT1 affords an efficient mechanism to restrict STAT1 activity by directly opposing its phosphorylation in the nucleus.
source: Thus, binding of PHLPP1 via its NTE to STAT1 affords an efficient mechanism to restrict its activity by directly opposing its phosphorylation in the nucleus (see Figure 8).
evidence: Inferred from the combined data showing NTE-mediated binding (Figure 7B-C) and nuclear function (Figure 6).

claim: The regulation of STAT1 by PHLPP1 occurs in the nucleus.
source: The regulation of STAT1 by PHLPP1 occurs in the nucleus, and we identify motifs in the phosphatase that control both the entry into (NLS) and exit from (NES) the nucleus.
evidence: Supported by the nuclear localization studies (Figure 6) and functional data showing nuclear targeting is required (Figure 6C).

claim: PHLPP1 has an NLS that controls entry into the nucleus.
source: The regulation of STAT1 by PHLPP1 occurs in the nucleus, and we identify motifs in the phosphatase that control both the entry into (NLS) and exit from (NES) the nucleus.
evidence: Directly supported by bioinformatics analysis (Figure 6D) and immunofluorescence data (Figure 6E-F).

claim: PHLPP1 has an NES that controls exit from the nucleus.
source: The regulation of STAT1 by PHLPP1 occurs in the nucleus, and we identify motifs in the phosphatase that control both the entry into (NLS) and exit from (NES) the nucleus.
evidence: Directly supported by bioinformatics analysis and immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Under unstimulated conditions, PHLPP1 localized primarily to the cytosol, suggesting masking of the NLS and exposure of the NES.
source: Under the 'unstimulated' conditions of our immunofluorescence, PHLPP1 localized primarily to the cytosol, suggesting masking of the NLS and exposure of the NES.
evidence: Inferred from immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3 showing cytosolic localization of full-length PHLPP1.

claim: Inputs that regulate the exposure of the NLS and NES are likely important regulators of PHLPP1 function.
source: Inputs that regulate the exposure of the NLS and NES are likely important regulators of PHLPP1 function.
evidence: Speculative statement by the authors based on the identification of NLS and NES.

claim: Transcriptomic data support a key role for PHLPP1 in the resolution of the inflammatory response specific to genes downstream of type II IFN signaling pathways.
source: Our transcriptomic data support a key role for PHLPP1 in the resolution of the inflammatory response specific to genes downstream of type II IFN signaling pathways.
evidence: Inferred from the RNA-Seq data in Figure 2 and gene ontology analysis.

claim: PHLPP1 can selectively discriminate between inflammatory promoters that are differentially regulated by distinct transcription factor families.
source: This suggests the possibility that PHLPP1 can selectively discriminate between inflammatory promoters that are differentially regulated by distinct transcription factor families.
evidence: Speculative statement by the authors based on the selective effects on STAT-regulated genes.

claim: Over 50% of the inflammatory genes that fail to properly resolve in macrophages from Phlpp1-/- mice contain a consensus STAT-binding motif in their proximal promoters.
source: Surprisingly, over 50% of the inflammatory genes that fail to properly resolve in the macrophages from Phlpp1-/- mice contain a consensus STAT-binding motif in their proximal promoters.
evidence: Directly supported by motif analysis data in Figure 2C-D showing 46% have STAT motifs and 26% have both STAT and IRF motifs.

claim: PHLPP1 is likely recruited to gene promoters through its association with STAT1.
source: Our studies have demonstrated a direct interaction between PHLPP1 and STAT1, thus it is highly likely that PHLPP1 is recruited to gene promoters through its association with STAT1.
evidence: Inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 7B-C showing direct interaction.

claim: Elevated STAT1 occupancy and delayed dismissal kinetics of STAT1 from its target promoters in Phlpp1-/- macrophages indicate a major function of PHLPP1-dependent dephosphorylation in termination of STAT1 signaling and its dismissal from chromatin.
source: Elevated STAT1 occupancy and delayed dismissal kinetics of STAT1 from its target promoters in Phlpp1-/- macrophages indicate a major function of PHLPP1-dependent dephosphorylation in termination of STAT1 signaling and its dismissal from chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from the ChIP data in Figure 3D-F showing enhanced and sustained STAT1 binding in Phlpp1-/- cells.

claim: Germline mutations that impair STAT1 function increase the susceptibility of otherwise healthy patients to mycobacterial and viral infection.
source: Germline mutations that impair STAT1 function, by reducing either Tyr701 phosphorylation (L706S) or DNA binding (Q463H and E320Q), increase the susceptibility of otherwise healthy patients to mycobacterial and viral infection (Chapgier et al., 2006; Dupuis et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Chapgier et al., 2006; Dupuis et al., 2001).

claim: Increased susceptibility to infection in patients with STAT1 mutations was proposed to arise because of reduced transcription of genes involved in bacterial and viral immunity from the GAS and ISRE promoters.
source: This increased susceptibility was proposed to arise because of reduced transcription of genes involved in bacterial and viral immunity from the GAS and ISRE promoters, respectively.
evidence: Represents interpretation from prior published work on STAT1 mutations.

claim: Genetic ablation of Stat1 on the background of a mouse with enhanced TLR4 signaling provides protection against LPS-induced toxemic death compared to mice with normal STAT1 levels.
source: Similarly, genetic ablation of Stat1 on the background of a mouse that has enhanced TLR4 signaling (because of deletion of Il6st, a key regulator of systemic inflammatory responses during LPS-mediated endotoxemia) provides protection against LPS-induced toxemic death compared to mice with normal STAT1 levels (Luu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Luu et al., 2014).

claim: PHLPP1 inhibitors could be explored as adjunctive therapies to antibiotics and supportive care of patients with Gram-negative sepsis.
source: Although the current study does not provide direct evidence that enhanced phosphorylation of STAT1 causes the protective effect of PHLPP1 loss on both E. coli-induced sepsis and LPS-induced endotoxemia in mice, our data indicate that PHLPP1 inhibitors could be explored as adjunctive therapies to antibiotics and supportive care of patients with Gram-negative sepsis, a leading cause of mortality in intensive care units.
evidence: Speculative therapeutic implication based on the protective effect of PHLPP1 loss in mouse models.

claim: Gram-negative sepsis is a leading cause of mortality in intensive care units.
source: Although the current study does not provide direct evidence that enhanced phosphorylation of STAT1 causes the protective effect of PHLPP1 loss on both E. coli-induced sepsis and LPS-induced endotoxemia in mice, our data indicate that PHLPP1 inhibitors could be explored as adjunctive therapies to antibiotics and supportive care of patients with Gram-negative sepsis, a leading cause of mortality in intensive care units.
evidence: Represents established medical knowledge.

claim: PHLPP1 was originally discovered for its function in suppressing growth factor signaling by dephosphorylating Akt on Ser473.
source: Originally discovered for its function in suppressing growth factor signaling by dephosphorylating Akt on the hydrophobic motif site, Ser473 (Gao et al., 2005), the repertoire of PHLPP1 substrates is continually expanding (Grzechnik and Newton, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Gao et al., 2005; Grzechnik and Newton, 2016).

claim: PHLPP1 is a bona fide tumor suppressor.
source: PHLPP1 is a bona fide tumor suppressor: its expression is frequently lost in cancer and its genetic ablation in a mouse model results in prostate neoplasia (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).

claim: PHLPP1 expression is frequently lost in cancer.
source: PHLPP1 is a bona fide tumor suppressor: its expression is frequently lost in cancer and its genetic ablation in a mouse model results in prostate neoplasia (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).

claim: Genetic ablation of PHLPP1 in a mouse model results in prostate neoplasia.
source: PHLPP1 is a bona fide tumor suppressor: its expression is frequently lost in cancer and its genetic ablation in a mouse model results in prostate neoplasia (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior published work (Chen et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2009).

claim: PHLPP1 dephosphorylation of Akt reduces the capacity of regulatory T cells to transduce T cell receptor signals.
source: PHLPP1 is also involved in the immune response, where its dephosphorylation of Akt reduces the capacity of regulatory T cells to transduce T cell receptor signals, a key function in T cell development (Patterson et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Patterson et al., 2011).

claim: Mice lacking PHLPP1 have enhanced chondrocyte proliferation as a result of increased Akt2 activity, diminished FoxO1 levels, and increased Fgf18 expression.
source: Additionally, mice lacking PHLPP1 have enhanced chondrocyte proliferation as a result of increased Akt2 activity, diminished FoxO1 levels, and increased Fgf18 expression, suggesting PHLPP1 inhibition could be a strategy to promote cartilage regeneration and repair (Bradley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Bradley et al., 2015).

claim: PHLPP1 inhibition could be a strategy to promote cartilage regeneration and repair.
source: Additionally, mice lacking PHLPP1 have enhanced chondrocyte proliferation as a result of increased Akt2 activity, diminished FoxO1 levels, and increased Fgf18 expression, suggesting PHLPP1 inhibition could be a strategy to promote cartilage regeneration and repair (Bradley et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative therapeutic implication from prior published work (Bradley et al., 2015).

claim: PHLPP1 suppresses receptor tyrosine kinase gene expression by a mechanism distinct from its effects on Akt.
source: PHLPP1 also suppresses receptor tyrosine kinase gene expression by a mechanism distinct from its effects on Akt, to influence growth factor signaling, including that mediated by the epidermal growth factor (EGF) receptor (Reyes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Reyes et al., 2014).

claim: PHLPP1 has a PH domain essential for dephosphorylation of protein kinase C (PKC).
source: Most notably, it has a PH domain essential for dephosphorylation of protein kinase C (PKC) (Gao et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Gao et al., 2008).

claim: PHLPP1 has a PDZ ligand necessary for Akt recognition.
source: a PDZ ligand necessary for Akt recognition (Gao et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Gao et al., 2005).

claim: PHLPP1 has a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) segment required for transcriptional regulation of receptor tyrosine kinases.
source: and a leucine-rich repeat (LRR) segment required for transcriptional regulation of receptor tyrosine kinases (Reyes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Reyes et al., 2014).

claim: PHLPP1 possesses an approximately 50 kDa N-terminal extension (NTE) of unknown function.
source: In addition, PHLPP1 possesses an approximately 50 kDa N-terminal extension (NTE) of unknown function.
evidence: Represents a structural feature of PHLPP1 that was previously uncharacterized.

claim: PHLPP1 has a > 10 fold lower catalytic rate compared to the closely related phosphatase PP2Cα.
source: Stoichiometric association with substrates by direct binding to the protein-interaction domains on PHLPP or common scaffolds (e.g. PDZ domain proteins such as Scribble; see Li et al., 2011) allows fidelity and specificity in PHLPP function, and may account for its > 10 fold lower catalytic rate compared to the closely related phosphatase PP2Cα (Sierecki and Newton, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior published work (Sierecki and Newton, 2014).

claim: PHLPP1 is an attractive pharmacological target for modulation of gene expression.
source: Given its transcriptional regulation of at least one family of genes (Reyes et al., 2014), PHLPP1 is an attractive pharmacological target for modulation of gene expression.
evidence: Speculative statement by the authors based on PHLPP1's transcriptional regulatory functions.
